lessons.title: Why Quantum Code Needs the Same Discipline as Any Production Code
lessons.chapterTitle: Software Engineering Practices for Quantum Code

slots.practicalActivity: A colleague says their Grover's-search notebook 'works' because it printed the right answer with highest probability once this morning. List two specific reasons that single run is not sufficient evidence the code is correct and will keep working, citing the three quantum-specific failure modes from this lesson (probabilistic output, hardware noise, SDK churn).
slots.deliverable: Your written list of two specific reasons, each explicitly citing one of the lesson's three named failure modes.

lessons.title: Project Structure for a Quantum Software Package
lessons.chapterTitle: Software Engineering Practices for Quantum Code

slots.practicalActivity: A teammate's module bell_state.py contains a function that builds the circuit, calls backend.run(), and returns the parsed counts, all in one function. Identify which two of this lesson's structural recommendations that function violates, then rewrite its signature (not its body) into separate construction/execution functions that fix both.
slots.deliverable: Your written identification of the two violated structural recommendations, plus the two rewritten function signatures.

lessons.title: Dependency Management for Quantum SDKs
lessons.chapterTitle: Software Engineering Practices for Quantum Code

slots.practicalActivity: Your team upgrades from qiskit==1.1.0 to qiskit==1.2.4. No import errors occur, but a statistical test that previously passed now fails by a wide margin. Walk through which two items from this lesson's upgrade checklist you'd check first, and explain why a loud-break assumption would have missed this entirely.
slots.deliverable: Your written walkthrough naming the two checklist items to check first, with an explanation of why assuming a loud break would have missed the problem.

lessons.title: Documentation Standards for Quantum Code
lessons.chapterTitle: Software Engineering Practices for Quantum Code

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite this docstring to include the quantum-specific fields this lesson argues are missing: def build_bell_pair(): """Builds a Bell pair circuit. Returns: A 2-qubit QuantumCircuit.""". You don't need to write the circuit code, just the improved docstring text, following this lesson's template (Circuit, Qubit roles, Expected measurement distribution, Validated against).
slots.deliverable: Your rewritten docstring text covering all four of the lesson's template fields.

lessons.title: Why Testing a Quantum Program Is Genuinely Different
lessons.chapterTitle: Testing & Debugging Quantum Programs

slots.practicalActivity: A teammate writes assert counts['00'] > 400 to test a Bell state circuit with 1024 shots, and says 'it's basically a statistical test since it's not exact equality.' Explain specifically what's missing from their test that a real statistical test would include, and rewrite their assertion into one with an explicit confidence level.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of what's missing (standard error and a stated confidence level) plus the rewritten statistical-test assertion.

lessons.title: Unit-Testing Circuit-Construction Logic
lessons.chapterTitle: Testing & Debugging Quantum Programs

slots.practicalActivity: Write out, in words (not full code), a construction test for a function build_qft_circuit(n_qubits) that should contain exactly one Hadamard gate per qubit plus a specific pattern of controlled-phase gates. State what you would assert and why none of those assertions would require actually running the circuit.
slots.deliverable: Your written description of the construction test's assertions, with reasoning for why each one needs no circuit execution.

lessons.title: Statistical Testing of Measurement Outcomes
lessons.chapterTitle: Testing & Debugging Quantum Programs

slots.practicalActivity: A circuit run for 1024 shots returns 512/512 exactly — a perfect split. Compute the z-score by hand (phat=0.5 exactly equals p0=0.5), then explain why this 'perfect' result passing trivially is not, by itself, stronger evidence of correctness than the lesson's own 540/1024 result passing.
slots.deliverable: Your z-score calculation for the 512/512 case and a written explanation of why a perfect split isn't stronger evidence than the lesson's passing 540/1024 result.

lessons.title: Debugging a Circuit That Gives Wrong Results
lessons.chapterTitle: Testing & Debugging Quantum Programs

slots.practicalActivity: A statistical test for a 2-qubit circuit expected to produce only '01' is failing. The statevector simulator shows the exact state |01⟩ with probability 1.0. Using this lesson's debugging order, explain what this tells you about where the bug is NOT located, and which debugging step you would move to next.
slots.deliverable: Your written diagnosis stating which causes are ruled out by the statevector check and which debugging step you would move to next.

lessons.title: Testing Lab
lessons.chapterTitle: Testing & Debugging Quantum Programs

slots.practicalActivity: In this lab's deliberately broken cx(i, 0) example (control and target swapped), explain in your own words why test_ghz_gate_sequence still passes even though the circuit is logically wrong, and why that's not a flaw in that specific test but a reason the suite needs the statevector test too.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of why the gate-sequence test passes on broken code, and why the statevector test is necessary to actually catch this bug.

lessons.title: Separating Circuit Logic From Execution Backend
lessons.chapterTitle: Quantum Software Architecture & Design Patterns

slots.practicalActivity: A function def measure_entanglement(n_qubits, shots=2048): ... builds a GHZ circuit, runs it on AerSimulator(), and returns a computed correlation statistic. Using this lesson's refactoring checklist, describe the three functions you'd split this into and what each one would take as parameters.
slots.deliverable: Your written description of the three split functions (construction, execution, analysis) with their parameter signatures.

lessons.title: The Backend-Abstraction Pattern
lessons.chapterTitle: Quantum Software Architecture & Design Patterns

slots.practicalActivity: A teammate wants to add get_queue_position() to the shared QuantumBackend interface so 'all backends have it.' Explain why this lesson would flag that as capability leakage, and propose where get_queue_position() should actually live instead.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of the capability-leakage problem and your proposed alternate location for the method.

lessons.title: Designing for Multiple SDKs: Qiskit & Q# Together
lessons.chapterTitle: Quantum Software Architecture & Design Patterns

slots.practicalActivity: Explain, in your own words, why QSharpAdapter calls a subprocess rather than importing a qsharp Python package directly in the same process as QiskitAdapter, and connect this back to the specific environment-isolation concern raised in Lesson 3 (dependency management).
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation connecting the subprocess boundary to Lesson 3's dependency-isolation concern.

lessons.title: Architecture Lab
lessons.chapterTitle: Quantum Software Architecture & Design Patterns

slots.practicalActivity: The lab's refactored estimate_ghz_fidelity still hardcodes the fidelity formula ('0'*n_qubits and '1'*n_qubits as the only 'correct' outcomes) inside fidelity_from_counts. Decide whether this is a structural problem this lab's refactor should have fixed, or a reasonable scope boundary, and justify your answer using this chapter's separation-of-concerns and over-engineering principles.
slots.deliverable: Your written verdict (structural problem or reasonable scope boundary) with justification citing this chapter's own principles.

lessons.title: Version Control Practices for Research Code
lessons.chapterTitle: Version Control & Reproducibility for Quantum Research

slots.practicalActivity: Six months after reporting a fidelity number, a colleague asks you to re-verify it, but you only remember it came from 'sometime last spring.' Walk through what this lesson's tagging convention would have needed to exist at the time for that re-verification to be possible today, and write the git commands you'd use now if it had.
slots.deliverable: Your written walkthrough of the tagging practice that was needed, plus the git commands for retrieving a properly tagged experiment.

lessons.title: Pinning SDK Versions — and Why It Matters More Here
lessons.chapterTitle: Version Control & Reproducibility for Quantum Research

slots.practicalActivity: A reported result's git tag exists, but no lockfile was ever committed alongside it — only a pyproject.toml with qiskit>=1.0 (a range, not an exact pin). Explain concretely what information is now missing to reproduce that result, even though the exact code commit is still retrievable.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of the specific missing information (the resolved transitive dependency tree) and why the exact commit alone is insufficient.

lessons.title: Recording Random Seeds, Shots & Backend Versions
lessons.chapterTitle: Version Control & Reproducibility for Quantum Research

slots.practicalActivity: A result record captures seed_simulator=42 and shots=1024 but not seed_transpiler. A later re-run with the recorded seed and shots still produces a visibly different fidelity number. Using this lesson's content, explain the most likely reason why, and write what the corrected experiment record should have included.
slots.deliverable: Your written diagnosis naming the missing seed_transpiler as the likely cause, plus the corrected experiment record's fields.

lessons.title: Reproducibility Lab
lessons.chapterTitle: Version Control & Reproducibility for Quantum Research

slots.practicalActivity: During the fire drill, uv sync succeeds and the checked-out commit is correct, but the reproduced fidelity is 0.89 instead of 0.97 — outside what this chapter's statistical tolerance would call consistent. List, in order, the first two things from this lesson's diagnostic steps you'd check, and explain why that order makes sense.
slots.deliverable: Your written ordered list of the first two diagnostic checks, with reasoning for why that specific order makes sense.

lessons.title: Profiling a Quantum-Classical Hybrid Program
lessons.chapterTitle: Performance & Resource Estimation in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: A teammate runs cProfile on their entire VQE script, including the real-hardware backend.run() calls, and concludes 'the bottleneck is backend.run(), so I need to optimize my code's call to it.' Explain what's wrong with that conclusion and what they should profile instead.
slots.deliverable: Your written explanation of the flawed conclusion and the correct profiling approach (separating queue wait, device execution, and classical time).

lessons.title: Estimating Circuit Resource Requirements Before Running
lessons.chapterTitle: Performance & Resource Estimation in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: A QAOA circuit has p=5 layers (so 2p=10 parameters) and will be optimized for 50 iterations at 1500 shots per circuit evaluation, using the parameter-shift rule. Compute the total shot budget for the full run, showing each step the same way this lesson's Worked Example 2 did.
slots.deliverable: Your step-by-step shot-budget calculation (evaluations per gradient, total executions, total shots) for the p=5 scenario.

lessons.title: Performance Lab
lessons.chapterTitle: Performance & Resource Estimation in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Using this lab's numbers, if the team instead kept 150 iterations and 4096 shots but switched to p=2 layers (4 parameters) instead of p=4, compute the new total shot budget and state whether it fits the 2,000,000-shot budget.
slots.deliverable: Your recomputed total-shot-budget calculation for p=2 and a stated verdict on whether it fits the 2,000,000-shot allocation.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Library Scope & Requirements
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Building a Quantum Software Library

slots.practicalActivity: This lesson's requirements document doesn't mention documentation standards (Lesson 4) as an explicit acceptance criterion for any module. Decide whether this is an oversight, or reasonably deferred to Lesson 23, justifying your answer using this lesson's own stated chapter plan. Then write one additional lesson-referenced acceptance-criteria line for the Bell/GHZ module covering something not already listed.
slots.deliverable: Your written judgment (oversight vs. deferred) with justification, plus your own additional acceptance-criteria line for the Bell/GHZ module.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build the Core Library & Tests
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Building a Quantum Software Library

slots.practicalActivity: The capstone's qaoa_shot_budget function doesn't account for the classical optimizer's own internal randomness (a separate seed, per Lesson 16). Decide whether this is a gap in the current implementation relative to Lesson 21's stated requirements, or out of scope for this specific function, and justify your answer by referring to what the function is actually meant to estimate.
slots.deliverable: Your written verdict (gap vs. out of scope) with justification tied to the function's actual estimation purpose.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build Documentation & Examples
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Building a Quantum Software Library

slots.practicalActivity: The README's 'Validated against' section states real IBM hardware validation hasn't happened yet. A user wants to run quantumlib's Grover module on real hardware anyway. Based on this lesson and Chapter 4, determine the minimum additions (not already provided by the library) they'd need to make to report a trustworthy, reproducible result from that run.
slots.deliverable: Your written list of the minimum additions needed (git tag, lockfile, experiment record with calibration timestamp) for a trustworthy hardware report.

lessons.title: Capstone: Wrap-Up & Code Review
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Building a Quantum Software Library

slots.practicalActivity: Using this lesson's distinction between a genuine gap and deliberately deferred scope, classify 'Real-hardware validation has not been performed for any module' from the known-limitations list: is it a gap, a deferred scope decision, or does it depend on information not given here? Justify your answer, then write your own one-paragraph 'known limitations' entry for one additional honest gap you'd flag in quantumlib.
slots.deliverable: Your written classification with justification, plus your own additional known-limitations entry for quantumlib.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can bring real software-engineering discipline to quantum code: structuring a package with separated construction/execution/analysis, writing tiered construction and statistical tests, abstracting backends so simulator and hardware runs use identical algorithm code, making experimental results fully reproducible via git tags, lockfiles, and recorded seeds, and estimating circuit resource requirements before paying for an expensive hardware run — all demonstrated in the course's own three-algorithm quantumlib capstone.
